summary: Hessonite is the honey-orange cinnamon garnet, known as Gomed in Vedic tradition, a stone of protection, ambition and grounded courage. Warm and steady.
intro: Hessonite is the orange to brownish-orange variety of grossular garnet, often compared to cinnamon, honey, or the color of a strong tea. Its distinctive feature is a swirly, oily internal look, sometimes described as treacle, caused by tiny crystal inclusions. This gives a slightly syrupy glow unlike the clean sparkle of other garnets. Sri Lanka has been the main source for centuries, while India and Brazil also produce stones. Hessonite is generally cut as cabochons or faceted gems, and it is both affordable and durable. It is especially well known in Indian astrology, where it is worn as a gem of the shadow planet Rahu.
history: The name hessonite comes from the Greek hesson, meaning inferior, in reference to its lower hardness and density compared to true hyacinth zircon, with which it was once confused. In Vedic astrology, hessonite is called Gomed, a Sanskrit name referring to a cow-hide color, and is one of the nine Navaratna gems, worn for Rahu, the north lunar node. Ancient Sri Lankan miners have recovered hessonite for many centuries, and the gem appears in the jewelry of South Asia. In Europe, the stone was sometimes called cinnamon stone. Today it is one of the most popular astrological gems.
meaning: In crystal and Vedic tradition, hessonite is a protective and ambitious stone. It is worn to guard against confusion and negative influences, and to help a person pursue goals with clarity. Practitioners link it to the Sacral, Root, and Solar Plexus chakras, associating it with creativity, groundedness, and confident drive. Many see it as a stone for people who feel stuck or scattered and want a focused, practical energy. In Vedic custom, Gomed is traditionally worn on the middle finger in a silver or panchadhatu setting, and often with the advice of an astrologer. Its warm color is also linked to social ease and to a friendly, cooperative manner.
howToUse: Wear hessonite as a ring or pendant to keep its protective energy close. Hold a stone during grounding meditation, with attention on the lower belly and base of the spine. Place a piece on your desk to support career goals. In the Vedic tradition, the stone is worn on the middle finger and chosen with guidance. In a grid, pair hessonite with carnelian and smoky quartz for grounding and ambition. Keep a small stone in a pocket for days of uncertainty.
care: Hessonite is Mohs 6.5 to 7 and fairly durable. Wash with lukewarm soapy water and a soft brush. Ultrasonic cleaners are usually safe for clean stones but avoid them for heavily included ones. Cleanse by running water, sunlight, moonlight, sound, or smoke. It is stable in sunlight. Store apart from harder gems to prevent scratches. Avoid sudden temperature changes and harsh chemicals.
identify: Authentic hessonite shows a swirly, oily look under magnification and a honey to reddish-orange color. Look-alikes include spessartine, citrine, orange zircon, and orange glass. Spessartine is brighter and cleaner; citrine is lighter and lacks the swirl effect. Dyed quartz and glass are sold as Gomed in some markets. Poorly cut stones may look dull. Hessonite is rarely treated, but certificates from labs are advised for astrological use.

faq.a: Gomed is the Sanskrit name for hessonite garnet in Vedic astrology. It is one of the nine Navaratna gems and is traditionally linked to Rahu, worn for protection and to support focus and ambition.
